author: ValWood
body:
I'm picking up an unexpected biological process prediction from a prediction pipeline:

@LisaMatthews could you take a look if you have experimental support for this (is so we can annotate)


Claude review:
is there any evidence that  human APEH is involved in translation termination?

Not really. As far as I can find, no experiment shows APEH taking part in translation termination. The link exists only as a database annotation.

Where the annotation comes from

NCBI Gene and UniProt both list APEH under the GO term "translational termination". On NCBI Gene its evidence code is TAS — Traceable Author Statement. That means a curator put it there; nobody measured it. The genuinely experimental annotations for APEH are things like proteolysis (IDA, Inferred from Direct Assay). 
[nih](https://ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/gene/?term=327)
The curator was Reactome. Its "Eukaryotic Translation Termination" pathway includes a step called "APEH hydrolyses NAc-Ser-protein", and that step carries the GO Biological Process translational termination (0006415). This is how the GO term reached APEH. 
[reactome](https://reactome.org/content/detail/R-HSA-5691510)
[reactome](https://reactome.org/content/detail/R-HSA-141671)
The paper Reactome cites for that step is about the enzyme's chemistry, not about ribosomes: APEH prefers substrates with acetylated methionine, alanine and serine residues. Hydrolysis produces an acetylated amino acid and a N-terminus protein (Jones et al. 1991). 
[wikipathways](https://classic.wikipathways.org/index.php/Pathway:WP1813)

Why it's a weak basis

Reactome seems to have added APEH as a processing step after the new protein is released, not as part of termination itself. Even that placement is doubtful. APEH's main known activity is the preferential hydrolysis of terminal acetylated amino acids from small acetylated peptides, not removing the acetylated N-terminus from newly made full-length proteins. Its other described roles are in breaking down oxidised proteins and short peptides. 
[reactome](https://reactome.org/content/schema/instance/browser/5691503)

I found no studies showing APEH binding ribosomes or eRF1/eRF3, or changing stop-codon readthrough or termination efficiency when knocked down. This was a quick search, so a recent ribosome-interactome or proteomics screen could have flagged it. The GO and UniProt annotation on its own, though, doesn't count as evidence.

If you're using GO enrichment, check the evidence code. TAS terms from Reactome tend to pull loosely connected enzymes into processes like this one.
title: Review of TAS on  APEH translation termination (Reactome)
